cards.front: What embryonic tissue supplies astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and ventricle-lining ependymal cells?
cards.back: The neural-tube neuroepithelium, mostly through radial glia that also made neurons.
cards.quote: Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells come from the neuroepithelium of the neural tube, mostly through the same pool of radial glia that made the neurons.
cards.section: One job, three birthplaces

cards.front: In the CNS, {{c1::oligodendrocytes}} wrap axons in myelin, a job done by myelinating Schwann cells in the PNS.
cards.quote: oligodendrocytes and myelinating Schwann cells both wrap axons in myelin, in the central and the peripheral nervous system respectively.
cards.section: One job, three birthplaces

cards.front: Satellite glia surrounding neuron cell bodies in peripheral ganglia arise from the {{c1::neural crest}}.
cards.quote: Schwann cells and satellite glia come from the neural crest, the cells that leave the edges of the closing neural tube
cards.section: One job, three birthplaces

cards.front: Why is a glial cell’s job alone a weak guide to whether a developmental mutation will remove it?
cards.back: Cells doing the same job can have different progenitors and early requirements. Ask where the cell was born and what its progenitor needed at that stage.
cards.quote: To predict which glia a gene or signal removes, ask where the cell was born and what its progenitor needed at that time.
cards.section: One job, three birthplaces

cards.front: A manipulation removes neural crest progenitors before peripheral glia form, while neural-tube progenitors remain intact. What happens to Schwann cells and satellite glia versus oligodendrocytes, and why?
cards.back: Schwann cells and satellite glia are lost first; oligodendrocytes are not directly removed. The peripheral glia require neural crest progenitors, whereas oligodendrocytes arise from neural-tube progenitors.
cards.quote: Schwann cells and satellite glia come from the neural crest, the cells that leave the edges of the closing neural tube
cards.section: One job, three birthplaces

cards.front: Why can a stain showing a glial cell’s shape and position fail to establish its embryonic ancestry?
cards.back: Shape and position do not follow descendants. An ancestry test marks a progenitor and checks whether its descendants inherit the mark.
cards.quote: But a stain shows a cell's shape and position. It cannot follow a cell's descendants, so it could not settle where any glial cell came from.
cards.section: How do you learn a cell's ancestry?

cards.front: Why does a Cre-activated reporter remain on in descendants after they stop expressing the gene that drove Cre?
cards.back: Cre removes a DNA stop sequence. Descendants inherit that permanent DNA change, so later expression of the original driver gene is unnecessary.
cards.quote: The change is in the DNA, so it is permanent, and every descendant inherits it, whatever genes the descendant uses later.
cards.section: How do you learn a cell's ancestry?

cards.front: In an inducible Cre fate map, a progenitor first expresses the driver gene after the tamoxifen window has closed and has no marked ancestor. Will its descendants acquire the reporter mark, and why?
cards.back: No. Only driver-expressing cells within the pulse window can acquire the mark; expressing the driver later does not activate this completed pulse.
cards.quote: Only cells expressing the gene during that window are marked, and, as with most pulses, only a fraction of those.
cards.section: How do you learn a cell's ancestry?

cards.front: Fate mapping in mice traces microglia mainly to the embryonic {{c1::yolk sac}}.
cards.back: This birthplace must be established separately in other species.
cards.quote: A dose of tamoxifen at about embryonic day 7.5 marked cells expressing Runx1 then, which were in the yolk sac.
cards.section: Microglia come from outside

cards.front: An early mouse fate-map pulse labels about a third of yolk-sac macrophages and adult microglia, but few blood cells. Why does that support mainly yolk-sac ancestry?
cards.back: The source itself was only partly labeled. Matching its labeled fraction supports mainly yolk-sac ancestry, rather than implying that only one-third of microglia came from it.
cards.why: This comparison cannot give an exact contribution or exclude a small share from another source.
cards.quote: Read against a source labeled at a third, it means most of them.
cards.section: Microglia come from outside

cards.front: In a two-source mouse fate-map model, yolk-sac founders are 30% labeled and blood founders 2% labeled. If each source supplies half of adult microglia, what labeled fraction is expected? Assume labeled and unlabeled founders expand alike.
cards.back: Expected labeled fraction = 0.5 × 30% + 0.5 × 2% = 16%. This assumes only these two sources and equal expansion of labeled and unlabeled founders.
cards.quote: If labeled and unlabeled founders expand alike, and there is no third source, the labeled share of microglia mirrors the mix of their sources
cards.section: Microglia come from outside

cards.front: Ncx1-null mouse embryos form yolk-sac macrophages but lack a heartbeat, circulation and brain microglia. Which step in establishing brain microglia does this result implicate?
cards.back: Arrival in the brain depends on early circulation. Progenitors form outside the brain but fail to reach it without blood flow; this does not isolate a brain-intrinsic Ncx1 function.
cards.quote: made yolk-sac macrophages but had no brain microglia, so the progenitors travel in through the early circulation.
cards.section: Microglia come from outside

cards.front: Mice lacking the receptor {{c1::CSF1R}} have few or no microglia.
cards.quote: Microglia also need the receptor CSF1R: mice without it have few or none.
cards.section: Microglia come from outside

cards.front: Why can blood-cell entry after irradiation mislead a claim about how microglia are normally maintained in healthy adult mice?
cards.back: Irradiation permits monocyte entry. In healthy adult mice, microglia renew themselves rather than being replaced by blood monocytes, so the disturbed condition cannot establish normal maintenance.
cards.quote: In healthy adult mice, microglia renew themselves and blood monocytes do not replace them.
cards.section: Microglia come from outside

cards.front: What three conditions frame the cytokine route to astrocytes in rodent cortex?
cards.back: A progenitor must remain available, the inducing signal must arrive, and the cell must be competent to read it. Signal availability alone is insufficient.
cards.why: The rodent cortical astrocyte route illustrates these conditions; they are not a complete account of every astrocyte.
cards.quote: A progenitor must still be there.
cards.section: Radial glia switch from neurons to glia

cards.front: How does early Notch–Hes signaling help rodent cortical progenitors make astrocytes later?
cards.back: Hes repressors suppress proneural genes, preserving progenitors through the neurogenic phase so they remain available for later signals. This alone does not make astrocytes.
cards.quote: It keeps a reserve of progenitors undifferentiated through the neurogenic phase, so cells are still there when the later signals arrive
cards.section: Radial glia switch from neurons to glia

cards.front: What signaling sequence links the shared cytokine-receptor subunit gp130 to astrocyte-gene activation in rodent cortical progenitors?
cards.back: gp130 activates JAK kinases; JAK phosphorylates STAT3, which pairs up, enters the nucleus and activates genes such as GFAP.
cards.quote: JAK phosphorylates STAT3, which pairs up, enters the nucleus and switches on astrocyte genes such as GFAP
cards.section: Radial glia switch from neurons to glia

cards.front: How can a signal activate a transcription factor without activating its target gene during development?
cards.back: The target binding site can remain methylated and inaccessible to that factor. Competence depends on the gene’s regulatory state as well as activation of the signaling pathway.
cards.quote: STAT3 is activated, but the GFAP gene does not answer.
cards.section: Radial glia switch from neurons to glia

cards.front: A cortical progenitor retains an accessible astrocyte-gene promoter, but its cytokine signal is blocked. Does promoter accessibility alone ensure cytokine-driven astrocyte-gene activation? What happens and why?
cards.back: No; cytokine-driven activation is not ensured. An accessible promoter provides competence, but the signal must still activate the transcription factor that reads it.
cards.quote: the cell becomes able to answer the same cytokine.
cards.section: Radial glia switch from neurons to glia

cards.front: In the proposed mouse cortical neuron-to-progenitor feedback, newborn neurons still supply cytokine but lose their Notch ligands. Assume nearby progenitors remain present with methylated GFAP sites. What happens to the astrocyte push, and why?
cards.back: It should weaken: cytokine alone cannot overcome the competence block. The proposed feedback combines neuron-supplied cytokine with Notch-induced NFIA that helps demethylate the GFAP promoter; preserving only the signal leaves that second rule unmet.
cards.quote: new neurons supply both the Notch ligands that unlock the GFAP site and the cytokine that the unlocked progenitors read.
cards.section: Radial glia switch from neurons to glia

cards.front: What does NFIA help change in mouse cortical precursors so cytokine-activated STAT3 can read the GFAP promoter?
cards.back: NFIA helps demethylate the GFAP promoter, conferring competence to respond.
cards.quote: induce NFIA, which helps demethylate the GFAP promoter so that cytokine-activated STAT3 can read it.
cards.section: Radial glia switch from neurons to glia

cards.front: What is the order of the two major outputs of the spinal pMN domain in mice and chicks?
cards.back: Motor neurons first, then oligodendrocyte precursors (OPCs).
cards.quote: In mice and chicks, pMN first makes motor neurons (see the motor neuron lesson) and then switches to making OPCs.
cards.section: Oligodendrocytes start in a ventral strip

cards.front: An Olig1/Olig2-null mouse lacks spinal oligodendrocytes. Predict its spinal motor-neuron phenotype and explain why the missing outputs need not mean that pMN progenitors died.
cards.back: Almost no spinal motor neurons are expected, because both outputs share the affected pMN domain. Its cells instead take other fates: first V2 interneurons and later astrocytes.
cards.quote: Mice lacking both Olig1 and Olig2 have almost no spinal motor neurons and no spinal oligodendrocytes.
cards.section: Oligodendrocytes start in a ventral strip

cards.front: What is the sequence of the three OPC source waves traced in mouse forebrain?
cards.back: A ventral domain, then the lateral and caudal ganglionic eminences, then the cortex after birth.
cards.quote: from a ventral domain, then from the lateral and caudal ganglionic eminences
cards.section: Oligodendrocytes start in a ventral strip

cards.front: After one mouse forebrain OPC wave is killed during development, adult OPC numbers recover. Does this establish that the waves have identical adult functions? What additional comparison would address that claim?
cards.back: No. The ablation result shows numerical compensation by remaining waves; it leaves functional interchangeability open. Compare adult functions after each wave’s removal alongside cell counts. The reasoning combines the compensation rule with the distinction between cell number and what cells do.
cards.quote: Whether the waves are interchangeable in what they do as adults is still open.
cards.section: Oligodendrocytes start in a ventral strip

cards.front: In the rat optic-nerve O-2A culture system, which fate appears in serum-free medium versus 10% fetal calf serum?
cards.back: Serum-free: oligodendrocytes. With 10% fetal calf serum: GFAP-positive type-2 astrocytes.
cards.quote: Cells carrying the surface marker A2B5 became oligodendrocytes in serum-free medium, carrying galactocerebroside (GC).
cards.section: One cell, two futures

cards.front: Why does observing two fates from a progenitor in culture not establish that it produces both in a living animal?
cards.back: Culture demonstrates possible fates under those conditions. Evidence from the living animal is needed to establish that both outputs actually occur there.
cards.quote: A clear counterpart of the type-2 astrocyte in the living animal has been hard to find, so treat it as a fate seen in a dish.
cards.section: One cell, two futures

cards.front: What is the difference between a medium instructing cell fate and selecting a pre-existing fate?
cards.back: Instruction redirects the same starting cells. Selection changes which already-decided cells survive or divide, changing the mixture without redirecting fate.
cards.quote: Serum might instruct each cell, or it might only select which already-decided cells survive.
cards.section: Instruct or select? A design problem

cards.front: Two media produce different glial fates. Design a clone-switch experiment that distinguishes redirection from selective survival or growth.
cards.back: Track individual clones, switch media at defined times, and measure identity, cell counts and divisions before and after. A clone changing fate without cell loss or compensatory divisions supports instruction. This combines the medium-switch rule with controls for survival, proliferation and identity.
cards.quote: A clone moved from serum to serum-free medium on day two that ends as oligodendrocytes, with no loss of cells and no extra divisions
cards.section: Instruct or select? A design problem

cards.front: In illustrative precursor-culture data, 91% express an astrocyte marker after two days in serum, yet only 6% end astrocyte-like after serum removal then; removal after three days leaves 82% astrocyte-like. Recovery is similar. What does marker expression fail to establish?
cards.back: Irreversible commitment. The earlier marker-positive state can still be redirected, whereas the later state is mostly fixed. Similar recovery argues against a simple explanation by selective death.
cards.quote: The choice could still be reversed after one to two days in serum, after which it became fixed
cards.section: Instruct or select? A design problem

cards.front: In a glial precursor culture, switching serum to serum-free medium on day two redirects fate. What experiment is needed before assuming the reverse switch remains effective until the same day?
cards.back: Make reciprocal switches from serum-free medium to serum at several times and assess final identity. Reversibility in one direction does not establish when the window closes in the other.
cards.quote: A reciprocal move, from serum-free to serum, tells you whether the window closes at the same time in both directions.
cards.section: Instruct or select? A design problem

cards.front: What developmental sequence connects neural crest cells to mature Schwann cells?
cards.back: Crest cell → Schwann cell precursor → immature Schwann cell → myelinating or non-myelinating Schwann cell.
cards.quote: crest cell, then Schwann cell precursor, then immature Schwann cell, then myelinating or non-myelinating Schwann cell.
cards.section: Schwann cells come from the crest, in steps

cards.front: How can axons support Schwann cell precursors that otherwise die in culture?
cards.back: Axonal neuregulin, read through ErbB2 and ErbB3, supports precursor survival and maturation into Schwann cells.
cards.quote: neuregulin, a growth factor on axons read by ErbB2 and ErbB3, can keep them alive and drive their maturation into Schwann cells.
cards.section: Schwann cells come from the crest, in steps

cards.front: After conditional ErbB2 deletion in mice, ventral-root Schwann cell nuclei fall from 51 to 5 per section; sciatic nerve counts change from 588 to 564. Calculate each percentage reduction relative to its control.
cards.back: Ventral root: (51 − 5) ÷ 51 × 100 = 90.2%, about 90%. Sciatic nerve: (588 − 564) ÷ 588 × 100 = 4.08%, about 4%; the reported sciatic change was not significant.
cards.quote: ventral-root Schwann cells fell from 51 to 5 per section, a loss of about 90%.
cards.section: Schwann cells come from the crest, in steps

cards.front: ErbB2 deletion is early in mouse spinal roots but late in sciatic nerve; only roots show major Schwann cell loss. How would you test whether deletion timing, rather than location, explains the difference?
cards.back: Compare early and late deletion within the same location, checking deletion timing and targeted precursor populations. The existing experiment confounds timing with place, including early targeting of boundary cap cells in roots. Combine that confounding rule with the rule that precursor requirements vary by developmental stage.
cards.quote: So the result does not fully separate when from where.
cards.section: Schwann cells come from the crest, in steps

cards.front: Why does showing that an axonal growth factor keeps glial precursors alive fail to prove that the cells compete for a limited supply?
cards.back: A survival requirement does not demonstrate scarcity or competition. Those claims need evidence that supply is limiting and cells compete for it.
cards.quote: these experiments did not test whether the supply is limiting and competed for, as NGF is for sympathetic neurons.
cards.section: Schwann cells come from the crest, in steps

cards.front: After a developmental mutation, adult glial counts look normal, but neighboring axons are reduced. How could you distinguish an early compensated glial loss from a later secondary effect of axon loss?
cards.back: Follow the glial lineage, its fate and cell counts across development alongside axon counts. An early glial deficit followed by recovery fits compensation; a deficit following axon loss fits a secondary effect. This combines the first-deficit rule with compensation and dependence on neighboring cells.
cards.quote: common causes are compensation, a change of fate, secondary effects of losing neighbouring cells or axons
cards.section: Putting it together

cards.front: A researcher uses mouse yolk-sac fate mapping to assign the same dominant microglial birthplace to adult zebrafish. What happens to that prediction, and why?
cards.back: It fails: adult zebrafish microglia come mainly from later definitive blood-forming sites, rather than the earliest wave. A birthplace established in one species must be demonstrated in another.
cards.quote: In zebrafish, adult microglia come mainly from later, definitive blood-forming sites rather than from the earliest wave
cards.section: Putting it together

cards.front: In an illustrative two-source microglia fate map, adult labeling is 30% and blood labeling is 2%. If true yolk-sac precursors were 40% labeled, what yolk-sac contribution fits? Assume equal expansion and no third source. Why not infer all from a macrophage proxy labeled at 30%?
cards.back: Solve 30 = 40f + 2(1 − f): f = (30 − 2) ÷ (40 − 2) = 0.7368, about 74%. This combines mixture weighting with the source-labeling caveat: the proxy and true founders can differ. It illustrates sensitivity, not a measured contribution.
cards.quote: The one-third labeling was measured on yolk-sac macrophages, not on these precursors.
cards.section: How sure is the microglia fate map?

cards.front: A developmental manipulation eliminates Schwann cell precursors before their descendants form. Besides Schwann cells, which outputs could be reduced, and why?
cards.back: Melanocytes, endoneurial fibroblasts and parasympathetic neurons could also be reduced. These precursors generate more than glia, so their removal can affect those additional descendants.
cards.quote: They also give rise to melanocytes, endoneurial fibroblasts and parasympathetic neurons, so a mutation that removes the precursors removes more than glia.
cards.section: What else Schwann cell precursors make
